subject: Hospitality
title: Price Anchoring on Menus
description: One-minute skill: Price Anchoring on Menus.

hook.text: A $65 steak on the menu makes a $38 steak look reasonable. The expensive item exists not to sell—but to anchor your perception.

buildup.text: Price anchoring is a cognitive bias: people judge prices relative to nearby numbers.

discovery.text: Restaurants place high-priced items at the top of sections. Everything below feels like a deal by comparison.

twist.text: Removing dollar signs from menus increases spending by 8%. '$29.00' feels like money leaving your wallet. '29' is just a number.

climax.text: The most profitable item on the menu is often the second-most-expensive. The anchor draws eyes; the neighbor captures orders.

punchline.text: The $65 steak exists to sell the $38 one. Anchoring makes everything else feel cheap.

quiz.question: Why do some restaurants remove dollar signs from menus?
options: Because it increases spending by about 8%—prices feel less like money leaving your wallet
